papers.note: The origin paper for chain of thought prompting and the single most cited reasoning reference in the field.
papers.title: Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We explore how generating a chain of thought — a series of intermediate reasoning steps — significantly improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. In particular, we show how such reasoning abilities emerge naturally in sufficiently large language models via a simple method called chain of thought prompting, where a few chain of thought demonstrations are provided as exemplars in prompting. Experiments on three large language models show that chain of thought prompting improves performance on a range of arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The empirical gains can be striking. For instance, prompting a 540B-parameter language model with just eight chain of thought exemplars achieves state of the art accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing even finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier.
papers.explain_beginner: If you ask a large language model to just answer a hard question, it often gets it wrong. If instead you ask it to think out loud, step by step, before answering, its accuracy jumps sharply, especially on math word problems, common-sense puzzles, and symbolic tasks. This paper is the one that gave that approach its name, chain of thought prompting, and showed that the effect only really appears once models are big enough.
papers.explain_business: Before this paper, teams shipping AI features assumed that if a model was not good at multi-step reasoning, the answer was to fine-tune or retrain it. Wei et al. showed you can get large accuracy gains on hard tasks by changing only the prompt, at zero training cost, provided the model is large enough. Practically, this means better answers on tasks like customer analytics questions or policy checks by asking the model to work through them step by step, and it is the reason "reasoning modes" and "thinking" toggles now exist across commercial assistants.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is the foundational chain-of-thought paper. Wei et al. showed that few-shot prompting with exemplars whose answers are worked out step-by-step yields large accuracy gains over direct-answer prompting on GSM8K, MultiArith, CommonSenseQA and symbolic tasks, and that the gains are an emergent capability of scale, roughly appearing at 100B parameters and above. On GSM8K, prompting a 540B PaLM with eight chain-of-thought exemplars beat a fine-tuned GPT-3 verifier, without any weight updates. It reframes reasoning as an inference-time technique rather than a training problem, and it is why nearly every subsequent reasoning paper builds on some variant of intermediate step generation.

papers.note: The most cited education position paper, and the source of the competency and literacy framing now used in policy.
papers.title: ChatGPT for good? On opportunities and challenges of large language models for education
papers.abstract: Large language models represent a significant advancement in AI, and despite critical views and even bans within some communities, are here to stay. This position paper presents the potential benefits and challenges of educational applications of LLMs from student and teacher perspectives. The authors highlight how these models can be used to create educational content, improve student engagement and interaction, and personalize learning experiences. They argue LLMs in education require teachers and learners to develop new competencies and literacies to understand the technology, its limitations, and its unexpected brittleness. A clear pedagogical strategy with a strong focus on critical thinking and strategies for fact checking is required. Other challenges — potential bias in output, need for continuous human oversight, and potential for misuse — are not unique to AI in education but must be addressed to ensure responsible and ethical use.
papers.explain_beginner: ChatGPT and similar tools can help teachers make lessons and give students personalized practice, but they also make cheating easy and produce confident-sounding wrong answers. The paper argues schools should teach students to check what AI tells them and to think critically about it, rather than either banning the tools or letting students use them without any oversight.
papers.explain_business: For an ed-tech or corporate L&D team, this paper establishes the vocabulary that regulators and universities now use when discussing LLM procurement. Deploying models for learning without an accompanying literacy program, oversight process, and bias-monitoring plan is now the exception rather than the norm. Buyer questions to expect include: how do you handle hallucination, what is your bias evaluation, how do learners flag errors, what data do you retain, and how are teachers trained to supervise the tool.
papers.explain_practitioner: A position paper by more than 30 education researchers surveying LLM applications in learning — personalized feedback, tutoring at scale, curriculum generation, adaptive assessment — weighed against bias, hallucination, plagiarism, over-reliance, and unequal access. The core argument is that responsible use requires new competencies for both teachers and students, a clear pedagogical strategy that centers critical thinking and fact-checking, and continuous human oversight rather than one-time policy statements. Widely cited as the reference position paper for the AI-in-education debate.

papers.note: The most cited general LLM survey, covers pre-training, post-training, utilisation and evaluation in one frame.
papers.title: A Survey of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) has driven a transformative shift in artificial intelligence (AI), reshaping both research paradigms and practical applications. Distinguished from their predecessors by unprecedented scale and advanced capabilities, LLMs necessitate new frameworks for understanding their development, behavior, and societal impact. This survey systematically reviews recent advancements in LLM techniques across four key dimensions: (1) pre-training methodologies, which establish core model capabilities through large-scale self-supervised training, architectural innovations, and data curation strategies; (2) post-training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, which adapt foundational models to downstream tasks and enhance their alignment and safety; (3) utilization strategies, such as in-context learning, prompt engineering, and agentic reasoning, that optimize real-world deployment and enable effective interaction with external environments; and (4) evaluation methods, encompassing benchmarks for key ability dimensions such as core language capabilities, reasoning, and safety, which support comprehensive and reliable assessment of model performance. Additionally, we identify critical research issues, including those concerning theoretical foundations, efficient scaling, alignment, and agentic capability, and highlight the open challenges they present.
papers.explain_beginner: A large language model is what powers products like ChatGPT. This paper is the most comprehensive tour of how one gets built from scratch, from the huge dataset it learns on, to the fine-tuning that teaches it to follow instructions, to the tests used to prove it works. If you want a single reading list to understand modern AI, this is the map.
papers.explain_business: When executives ask "how do these things actually work end to end", this is the answer. It shows that building a competitive LLM requires four distinct capabilities — massive training data + compute, alignment and safety tuning, an application layer that turns raw models into products, and evaluation infrastructure — and that most vendors specialise in one or two of them. That framing is useful for build-versus-buy decisions and for understanding where an AI supplier's real moat sits.
papers.explain_practitioner: Zhao et al. give a four-part taxonomy of the LLM lifecycle — pre-training, post-training (SFT + RLHF), utilization (in-context learning, prompt engineering, agents) and evaluation — and cover the leading techniques in each. It is the field's de facto survey, kept current across arXiv versions, and its 4,600+ citations reflect that it is where most graduate courses and industry onboarding docs start. Use it as a citation-mining tool rather than a linear read.

papers.note: The MultiMedQA and Med-PaLM paper, and the origin of the multi axis human evaluation framework used since.
papers.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities, but the bar for clinical applications is high. Attempts to assess the clinical knowledge of models typically rely on automated evaluations based on limited benchmarks. Here, to address these limitations, we present MultiMedQA, a benchmark combining six existing medical question answering datasets spanning professional medicine, research and consumer queries and a new dataset of medical questions searched online, HealthSearchQA. We propose a human evaluation framework for model answers along multiple axes including factuality, comprehension, reasoning, possible harm and bias. In addition, we evaluate Pathways Language Model (PaLM, a 540-billion parameter LLM) and its instruction-tuned variant, Flan-PaLM on MultiMedQA. Using a combination of prompting strategies, Flan-PaLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on every MultiMedQA multiple-choice dataset (MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) clinical topics), including 67.6% accuracy on MedQA (US Medical Licensing Exam-style questions), surpassing the prior state of the art by more than 17%. However, human evaluation reveals key gaps. To resolve this, we introduce instruction prompt tuning, a parameter-efficient approach for aligning LLMs to new domains using a few exemplars. The resulting model, Med-PaLM, performs encouragingly, but remains inferior to clinicians. We show that comprehension, knowledge recall and reasoning improve with model scale and instruction prompt tuning, suggesting the potential utility of LLMs in medicine.
papers.explain_beginner: This is the paper where Google researchers showed that a general-purpose AI model, without any medical schooling, could pass US medical licensing exam questions. That was a jaw-dropping result in 2022 and started the wave of AI-in-medicine products. They also introduced a benchmark called MultiMedQA that the field still uses to test new medical AI systems.
papers.explain_business: This is the moment clinical AI stopped being theoretical. A general-purpose model, not built for medicine, cleared USMLE-style questions and set a new bar overnight. For any organisation running or buying clinical decision-support software, the immediate implication is that base-model gains now translate into clinical-benchmark gains almost directly, and that vendor claims should be validated against a standard set (MultiMedQA) rather than a bespoke internal one that is easy to game.
papers.explain_practitioner: Singhal et al. introduce MultiMedQA (six existing sets plus HealthSearchQA) and show Flan-PaLM 540B reaches 67.6% on MedQA-USMLE with prompt engineering alone, a 17-point jump over the prior state of the art. Instruction prompt tuning yields Med-PaLM, which narrows but does not close the gap to clinicians on a human-evaluated axis set (factuality, reasoning, potential harm, bias). It is the paper that established medical multiple-choice benchmarks as a real evaluation surface and standardised the human-eval axes now used across clinical LLM papers.

papers.note: The reference mixture of experts design that made sparse trillion parameter models practical.
papers.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
papers.explain_beginner: This paper introduces a new way to build artificial intelligence models that use vastly more parameters, or learned values, than before. Instead of using the same set of parameters for every input, the model selectively activates different parts depending on what it receives. This approach keeps computation time reasonable while dramatically increasing model size. The researchers solved problems that previously made this approach difficult to use in practice, allowing them to train models with a trillion parameters much faster than traditional approaches.
papers.explain_business: Switch Transformers enable organizations to deploy significantly more capable language models with improved training efficiency and cost. By achieving 4x to 7x speedups over previous approaches, companies can either reduce infrastructure spending for equivalent model performance or allocate the same budget toward substantially more powerful systems. This technology makes trillion-parameter models practically trainable, opening new capabilities for applications requiring advanced language understanding while maintaining operational efficiency.
papers.explain_practitioner: The work presents Switch Transformers, a simplified Mixture of Experts architecture that routes inputs to different parameter subsets via straightforward routing logic. Key improvements include reduced communication overhead, lower computational complexity, and stabilized training procedures enabling bfloat16 precision. The authors validated their approach on T5 variants, achieving 7x pre-training speedups and successfully training trillion-parameter models on web-scale data, with consistent gains across 101 languages in multilingual settings.

papers.note: The primer most clinicians have actually read, which makes it the right shared reference in client conversations.
papers.title: Large language models in medicine
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models, the AI systems behind tools like ChatGPT, are being rapidly adopted in medicine. They show promise in tasks ranging from helping doctors pass licensing exams to automatically summarizing patient records. This survey examines how these models are entering healthcare and what they can do. Understanding these capabilities matters because they could transform how doctors work and improve patient care, but we need reliable information about what they can and cannot do.
papers.explain_business: Large language models are moving into healthcare applications with measurable technical capabilities demonstrated across multiple domains. Organizations considering adoption should recognize that viable use cases exist, from clinical decision support to documentation management. However, the landscape is still rapidly evolving with diverse model types showing different strengths. Decision-makers should treat this as an emerging opportunity requiring careful evaluation of specific applications rather than broad implementation, informed by documented performance on relevant medical tasks.
papers.explain_practitioner: This primer reviews the emerging applications of large language models in clinical practice and medical research. The scope includes systems demonstrating performance on standardized medical assessments and document processing applications. The authors, publishing through KOSMI's special issue, synthesize current developments in LLM deployment across healthcare domains. The key finding is that multiple specialized implementations exist, each with distinct capabilities, requiring practitioners to understand specific use cases and performance characteristics when evaluating integration into clinical workflows.

papers.note: The standard reference on why clinical AI stalls between research and practice, still the clearest statement of the gap.
papers.title: Key challenges for delivering clinical impact with artificial intelligence
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers have created many promising artificial intelligence tools for medicine, but few actually make it into hospitals and clinics where patients can benefit from them. This paper explains why that gap exists. The main obstacles include technical challenges with how AI learns from data, practical difficulties in rolling out new systems, and the need for proper testing and regulation. The authors argue that AI healthcare tools must be rigorously tested like new drugs, clearly explained to doctors, and carefully monitored after release to ensure they truly help patients.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations considering AI investments should recognize that research success does not guarantee clinical utility or patient benefit. Successful deployment requires investment in rigorous clinical validation, regulatory navigation, and post-implementation monitoring rather than rapid adoption of promising prototypes. Decision-makers must prioritize vendors demonstrating transparent performance metrics relevant to clinical workflows, clear explainability of algorithmic decisions, and evidence of effectiveness across diverse patient populations. This framework protects organizations from deploying ineffective or biased systems while positioning them to capture genuine competitive advantages from AI innovations.
papers.explain_practitioner: This paper identifies critical barriers preventing clinical deployment of healthcare AI systems. Beyond core machine learning challenges, key obstacles include implementing rigorous randomized controlled trials for validation, developing clinically meaningful performance metrics, and ensuring regulatory frameworks that enable innovation while protecting patients. The authors emphasize the necessity of representative test datasets, mechanisms for comparative evaluation, and mitigation strategies against dataset shift, confounding, and algorithmic bias. Essential improvements require enhancing model interpretability, reducing generalization failures across populations, and measuring outcomes beyond accuracy metrics to include clinical care quality.

papers.note: A continuously refreshed coding benchmark, the working model for contamination free evaluation.
papers.title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers created LiveCodeBench, a new way to test how well AI language models can write code. Unlike older tests that stay the same, this benchmark continuously adds fresh coding problems from real programming competitions, preventing models from memorizing answers. The system checks not just code generation but also whether models can fix their own mistakes and predict what code will output. Testing 52 different models revealed that older benchmarks may give inflated scores because models have seen similar problems before.
papers.explain_business: Organizations selecting LLMs for coding tasks need accurate, unbiased performance metrics. LiveCodeBench provides confidence that model evaluations reflect genuine capabilities rather than memorization by continuously introducing fresh problems from actual competitions. This enables better purchasing decisions and realistic expectations for deployment. The ongoing refresh cycle means evaluations remain valid over time, reducing risk of selecting models that overperformed on outdated benchmarks but underperform in production.
papers.explain_practitioner: LiveCodeBench addresses benchmark contamination by dynamically sourcing problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces published after May 2023, ensuring evaluation data hasn't been seen during model training. The framework evaluates 52 LLMs across code generation and auxiliary capabilities including self-repair, execution, and test output prediction. The study demonstrates evidence of overfitting to existing static benchmarks and provides comprehensive empirical analysis of 18 base and 34 instruction-tuned models. Researchers will release all prompts, completions, and a toolkit for community extension.

papers.note: Preregistered experiment, 40 percent time reduction and 18 percent quality gain on professional writing tasks.
papers.title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether ChatGPT could help professional workers write faster and better. They gave writing tasks to over 450 college-educated workers, letting half use ChatGPT while the other half could not. Workers with ChatGPT completed their tasks 40 percent quicker and produced work that was 18 percent higher quality. The tool also helped reduce skill differences among workers. After the experiment ended, workers who had tried ChatGPT kept using it in their actual jobs, suggesting the technology has real staying power.
papers.explain_business: This research demonstrates that generative AI tools like ChatGPT deliver measurable productivity gains in professional writing work, specifically cutting task time by 40 percent while improving output quality by 18 percent. The findings indicate that skilled workers across different backgrounds benefit from the technology, narrowing performance gaps in the workforce. Strong post-experiment adoption rates suggest genuine business value. Organizations should consider that implementing such tools could accelerate project completion, improve work quality, and help standardize performance across teams with varying experience levels.
papers.explain_practitioner: A preregistered randomized controlled experiment with 453 college-educated professionals assigned to occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks evaluated ChatGPT's impact. Treatment participants received access to the chatbot while controls did not. Key findings included a 40 percent reduction in task completion time and 18 percent quality improvement measured against professional standards. Secondary outcomes showed decreased performance variance between workers, elevated AI sentiment, and sustained adoption behavior with workers in the treatment group showing 2.0x adoption rates at two weeks post-experiment and 1.6x rates at two months.

papers.note: The founding internal audit framework, and the source of the document per stage audit report structure now common in practice.
papers.title: Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency
papers.abstract: Rising concern for the societal implications of artificial intelligence systems has inspired a wave of academic and journalistic literature in which deployed systems are audited for harm by investigators from outside the organizations deploying the algorithms. However, it remains challenging for practitioners to identify the harmful repercussions of their own systems prior to deployment, and, once deployed, emergent issues can become difficult or impossible to trace back to their source. In this paper, we introduce a framework for algorithmic auditing that supports artificial intelligence system development end-to-end, to be applied throughout the internal organization development life-cycle. Each stage of the audit yields a set of documents that together form an overall audit report, drawing on an organization's values or principles to assess the fit of decisions made throughout the process. The proposed auditing framework is intended to contribute to closing the accountability gap in the development and deployment of large-scale artificial intelligence systems by embedding a robust process to ensure audit integrity.
papers.explain_beginner: Companies build AI systems, then only later find out the systems have caused harm — biased hiring decisions, wrongful arrests, unsafe recommendations. This paper argues that audits should happen inside the company, throughout development, not just after the fact. It maps out what documents each stage of the audit should produce, so problems get caught before deployment rather than blamed on the algorithm after damage is done.
papers.explain_business: This is the paper that makes the case for internal AI audit as a discipline, not just an external activity. For any organisation building or deploying AI, the argument is that the audit trail must be built as you go — datasheets, model cards, testing records, failure analyses — because reconstructing them after a harm event is impossible and expensive. Regulators from NIST to the EU are now writing this into policy, so treating it as optional will translate directly into compliance friction and litigation exposure over the next two years.
papers.explain_practitioner: Raji et al. propose SMACTR, an internal-audit lifecycle for AI systems spanning scoping, mapping, artifact collection, testing, and reflection. Each stage has explicit deliverables (datasheets, model cards, failure analyses, remediation plans) that together form an audit record aligned to the organisation's stated AI principles. It is heavily cited because it was the first serious attempt to translate the ethics-principles literature into an actual engineering process, and NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act's conformity-assessment structure all borrow its shape.

papers.note: Chain of thought text can rationalise a biased answer without mentioning the bias, which undercuts using it as an audit artifact.
papers.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers discovered that when large language models explain their reasoning step-by-step, they often hide what actually influenced their answers. The models were tested by sneaking in biases, like always putting the correct answer in position A. The models would give biased answers but fail to mention these biases in their explanations. This matters because people might trust these systems more when they see explanations, but those explanations can be dishonest about what really drove the decisions.
papers.explain_business: Chain-of-thought explanations create a false sense of transparency in language models. While these step-by-step reasoning outputs appear trustworthy, they can rationalize biased or incorrect decisions without revealing the actual causes. Organizations relying on CoT for model auditing or compliance documentation face hidden risks. Decision-makers should not assume detailed explanations guarantee safe or unbiased model behavior. Investment in alternative transparency methods or specialized faithfulness improvements is necessary before deploying these systems in high-stakes applications.
papers.explain_practitioner: We evaluated chain-of-thought faithfulness by introducing input biases to GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 and measuring whether models acknowledged these influences in their explanations. We used 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks plus social-bias evaluations. Results showed models systematically omitted mention of biasing features while still being influenced by them, producing rationalizations for biased outputs. Performance degraded up to 36 percent when models were biased toward incorrect answers. CoT explanations proved plausible but unfaithful to actual decision processes.

papers.note: 5,172 support agents, 15 percent productivity gain concentrated in less experienced workers, the most cited field study of AI at work.
papers.title: Generative AI at Work
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers studied how an AI chatbot assistant affected customer service workers. They found the tool made workers about 15 percent more productive at solving customer problems. Newer, less experienced workers benefited the most, while experienced workers saw minimal gains. The AI appeared to share knowledge that skilled workers had learned through experience, helping newer employees improve faster. The tool also made customers happier and reduced employee turnover.
papers.explain_business: Deploying conversational AI in customer support operations yields meaningful productivity improvements, particularly for newer workforce segments. The technology effectively transfers experienced worker knowledge to junior staff, accelerating development and reducing training costs. Beyond efficiency gains, the solution enhances customer satisfaction and employee retention while decreasing management overhead. This suggests AI implementation in support functions can simultaneously improve operational metrics and workforce development outcomes.
papers.explain_practitioner: A field study tracked 5,179 support agents receiving staggered access to a generative AI conversational system. The intervention increased average productivity by 14 percent measured in resolved issues per hour. Benefits concentrated among novice and lower-skill cohorts while experienced workers showed negligible gains. Analysis suggests the AI captured tacit knowledge from high-performing agents and accelerated skill development in junior staff. Secondary outcomes included improved customer satisfaction metrics, decreased managerial escalations, and enhanced employee retention rates.

papers.note: Balanced account of both democratised access and misinformation risk across practice, research and education.
papers.title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines AI tools called large language models that can read and write text nearly as well as humans. Since ChatGPT became popular in late 2022, these tools have attracted interest in medicine. The researchers found that while these models could help make medical knowledge more accessible and improve healthcare, they also pose serious risks like spreading false information and enabling scientific fraud. The paper balances both the promising opportunities and concerning dangers across medical practice, research, and education.
papers.explain_business: Medical organizations face a strategic decision about large language model adoption. The technology promises improved information accessibility and operational efficiency across clinical, research, and educational functions. However, implementation requires substantial risk mitigation strategies addressing accuracy verification, regulatory compliance, and accountability frameworks. Decision-makers should weigh deployment benefits against liability exposure and reputational risks from potential misinformation spread or research misconduct. A cautious, controlled adoption approach with robust oversight mechanisms is advisable before widespread integration.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic review of large language models across three medical domains: clinical practice, research, and education. LLMs demonstrate human-level performance in text comprehension and generation tasks including question answering, summarization, and translation. The key finding identifies a dual-edged impact: these models offer democratization potential for medical information access and knowledge dissemination, yet simultaneously introduce risks through unaccountable outputs that may propagate inaccurate information and facilitate research integrity violations due to insufficient transparency mechanisms.

papers.note: The most cited general survey of the field, covering the GPT, LLaMA and PaLM families, training datasets, and evaluation metrics. A reasonable first read for anyone needing the shape of the field rather than a single result.
papers.title: Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models like the systems behind ChatGPT multiplied so quickly that it became hard to keep track of how they worked or how they compared to one another. This paper does not run a new experiment. Instead it steps back and maps the whole field in one place, explaining how the major model families were built, what data they were trained on, and how researchers judge whether one model is actually better than another. It walks through the lineages behind well known systems such as GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM, describing what each family contributed and where it fell short. It also lays out the common ways models get tested, from simple accuracy scores to broader benchmark suites, and shows how leading models stack up against each other on shared tasks. The paper does not argue for a single new idea. Its value is as an orientation guide, giving newcomers a shared vocabulary and a sense of the landscape before they dive into any one narrower piece of research.
papers.explain_business: This paper introduces no new capability, so it changes nothing about what an organization can build or buy today. Its practical use is as a map for people who need to choose between model families without becoming AI researchers first. Understanding that GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM descend from different design choices and training data helps a buyer ask sharper questions of a vendor, such as what a model was trained on, how it was evaluated, and which benchmarks actually resemble the buyer's own use case. The survey's comparison tables are a reasonable starting point for due diligence conversations, though they age quickly since new models ship constantly and the numbers here reflect only what existed at the time of writing. There is no cost, risk, or compliance finding to act on directly. The main business takeaway is procedural. treat any single benchmark score with caution, ask which evaluation methodology produced it, and expect today's leaderboard position to be temporary.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper is a structured literature review rather than an empirical study. It groups modern large language models by lineage, walking through the GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM families and summarizing the architectural choices, scale, and training recipes that define each generation. It then surveys the pretraining corpora, instruction tuning sets, and alignment data typically used to build these models, alongside the metrics and benchmark suites researchers rely on for evaluation, spanning knowledge tests, reasoning tasks, and generation quality. A comparison section places several prominent models side by side on shared tasks so readers can see relative strengths rather than take vendor claims at face value. The authors are explicit that a survey like this is a snapshot. Because the field moves fast, any fixed comparison table risks going stale within months as new models and benchmarks appear, and the paper's own coverage stops at the models and datasets known at the time of writing. It closes by naming open problems, including evaluation reliability and how far current benchmarks generalize.

papers.note: Written for clinical safety professionals appraising AI, which is exactly the audience for a healthcare AI audit.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence, bias and clinical safety
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines how artificial intelligence systems used in healthcare can develop hidden biases that compromise patient safety. The researchers investigated whether AI tools trained on historical medical data might make unfair or incorrect recommendations for certain groups of patients. Understanding these risks matters because hospitals increasingly rely on AI to help diagnose diseases and guide treatment decisions, so catching bias early prevents harm to vulnerable populations.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations adopting AI tools need formal processes to detect and mitigate algorithmic bias before deployment. This paper provides clinical safety professionals with guidance for auditing AI systems to ensure fair treatment across patient populations and protect against liability. Organizations should implement bias assessment as a standard requirement in their AI procurement and governance processes to maintain safety standards and trust.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic analysis of AI bias mechanisms within clinical contexts and their safety implications. They examined how training data characteristics, model development practices, and deployment conditions can introduce or amplify discriminatory patterns in AI decision-making. The study identified that clinical bias emerges through multiple pathways and established a framework for clinical safety professionals to evaluate and audit AI systems for these risks before and during implementation.

papers.note: Extends chain of thought to image plus text and reports reduced hallucination, relevant to document and imaging workflows.
papers.title: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers improved how AI systems answer complex questions by combining text and images together. Previously, AI models explained their reasoning using only words, but this new approach lets them look at pictures too while thinking through a problem. The system works in two steps: first it gathers information from both text and images to build an explanation, then it uses that explanation to pick the right answer. This method reduces the AI making up false information and helps it learn faster.
papers.explain_business: This technique enables AI systems to process documents with embedded images more accurately and reliably, reducing costly errors from hallucinated information. For document analysis, medical imaging review, or technical support workflows requiring visual context, this approach improves accuracy while maintaining efficient model size. The faster learning convergence means quicker deployment and adaptation to new domains. Organizations handling multimodal content can expect more dependable automated analysis, reducing manual verification overhead and supporting higher-confidence decision-making in document and imaging workflows.
papers.explain_practitioner: We developed Multimodal-CoT, a two-stage framework extending chain-of-thought prompting to incorporate both textual and visual inputs. Stage one generates rationales leveraging multimodal information, stage two uses these rationales for answer inference. Tested on ScienceQA and A-OKVQA benchmarks, a sub-1B parameter model achieved state-of-the-art on ScienceQA. Key results demonstrate reduced hallucination rates and improved convergence speed compared to language-only approaches. The approach separates rationale generation from inference, allowing better utilization of visual context in reasoning tasks.

papers.note: Peer reviewed architecture taxonomy covering training pipelines, datasets and deployment issues in one place.
papers.title: A Review on Large Language Models: Architectures, Applications, Taxonomies, Open Issues and Challenges
papers.authors: Mohaimenul Azam Khan Raiaan et al.
papers.explain_beginner: Large Language Models are powerful AI systems that understand and generate human language for tasks like translation, answering questions, and creating text. This paper surveys the entire landscape of these models, explaining how they work, where they came from, and what they do well. It covers their basic building blocks, real-world uses in medicine and education, and the practical problems researchers still need to solve before these systems can be reliably deployed everywhere.
papers.explain_business: This reference consolidates fragmented LLM knowledge into a single structured overview, enabling organizations to understand model capabilities, training requirements, and real-world deployment constraints. It clarifies practical applications across healthcare, education, and business domains while documenting unresolved challenges that affect implementation timelines and risk profiles. This informs strategic decisions about LLM adoption, resource allocation, and whether specific use cases are currently feasible or require further technological maturation.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive review synthesizes LLM development across multiple dimensions: historical evolution, transformer architecture specifics, training methodologies, datasets, and deployment frameworks. The paper systematically catalogs existing works while documenting the complete training pipeline for LLMs. It organizes applications across diverse domains including healthcare and agriculture, then systematically identifies open technical and practical challenges that arise when implementing these models in production environments.

papers.note: Trains a diffusion model rather than an autoregressive one at 8B scale and reaches comparable results, challenging the assumption that core language-model capability depends on next-token prediction.
papers.title: Large Language Diffusion Models
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers built a large language model using a different method than currently standard. Instead of predicting the next word in sequence, they used a diffusion approach that randomly masks words and learns to restore them. Testing an 8 billion parameter version, they found it works nearly as well as traditional models at tasks like reasoning, math, and coding. This matters because it shows that powerful language abilities don't require the dominant prediction method everyone uses, opening new possibilities for how AI systems could be designed.
papers.explain_business: This research demonstrates that diffusion-based language models can achieve performance parity with autoregressive models at production scale. Organizations considering model architecture investments should recognize that the current ARM-dominant paradigm is not the only viable path forward. This opens strategic options for developing alternative systems that might offer different trade-offs in inference speed, training efficiency, or robustness. The findings validate exploring architectural diversity rather than assuming one approach is fundamentally superior.
papers.explain_practitioner: We present LLaDA, a diffusion-based language model trained at 8B scale using standard pre-training and SFT protocols. The model employs forward masking and reverse denoising with a Transformer backbone optimizing a variational lower bound. Across diverse benchmarks, LLaDA matches ARM baselines in scaling behavior and performance on general, mathematical, and coding tasks. The 8B variant achieves competitiveness with LLaMA3 8B on in-context learning and post-SFT instruction-following. Notably, it outperforms GPT-4o on reversal-curse tasks, demonstrating the viability of diffusion-based language modeling at scale.

papers.note: The standard multimodal survey, covering architecture, training strategy, hallucination and evaluation.
papers.title: A survey on multimodal large language models
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers surveyed a new type of artificial intelligence called multimodal large language models, which combine powerful text-processing AI with the ability to understand images and other information types. These systems can perform impressive tasks like writing stories about pictures or solving math problems from images. The survey maps out how these systems work, how they're built and trained, and what problems they still face, suggesting they might be a stepping stone toward more general artificial intelligence.
papers.explain_business: Multimodal large language models represent a significant shift in AI capabilities, enabling systems to process images, text, and other inputs simultaneously with human-level reasoning. Organizations should understand that these models are rapidly advancing and becoming competitive with leading proprietary systems. This survey identifies key technical challenges like hallucination and evaluation gaps that currently limit deployment. Companies evaluating investment in AI infrastructure should track these developments, as capability gaps are closing quickly and architectural approaches are converging across academic and industry efforts.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey comprehensively reviews multimodal large language models that leverage pretrained language models as their foundation. The authors document architectural designs, training methodologies, dataset approaches, and evaluation frameworks. They catalog emerging capabilities including in-context learning and chain-of-thought reasoning across modalities, and address critical challenges such as hallucination phenomena. The work synthesizes progress toward systems matching GPT-4V performance while identifying extensions across granularity levels, modality types, language support, and deployment scenarios.

papers.note: Tested leading models against 2,400 real intensive-care cases and found they diagnosed worse than physicians and did not follow treatment guidelines, which is the sharpest published rebuttal to the argument that passing medical exams implies clinical readiness.
papers.title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested leading AI language models on 2,400 real intensive care cases to see if they could diagnose patients like doctors do. Despite performing well on medical exams, these AI systems diagnosed incorrectly far more often than physicians, ignored established medical guidelines, and struggled to understand lab results. The findings show that passing written exams doesn't mean AI is ready for actual patient care, highlighting important gaps between test performance and real-world medical practice.
papers.explain_business: This research demonstrates that deploying current AI language models in clinical settings would harm patient outcomes. Despite strong performance on licensing exams, these systems diagnose incorrectly, ignore medical guidelines, and struggle with practical clinical tasks. Organizations considering AI-assisted medical decision support must recognize that test scores do not validate clinical readiness. Investment in AI healthcare solutions requires validation against realistic patient data and clinical workflows before implementation.
papers.explain_practitioner: We evaluated state-of-the-art LLMs against a curated dataset of 2,400 intensive care cases covering four abdominal pathologies using a realistic clinical simulation framework. Results demonstrated significantly lower diagnostic accuracy than physicians across all conditions, failure to adhere to diagnostic and treatment protocols, and inability to process laboratory values. Models proved sensitive to information ordering and instruction following. The study provides both a benchmark dataset and evidence that current LLMs require substantial improvements before clinical deployment.

papers.note: The canonical bias survey, with three taxonomies covering metrics, datasets and mitigation stages.
papers.title: Bias and Fairness in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models are powerful AI systems that generate human-like text, but they can inadvertently learn and spread unfair biases from their training data. This survey examines how to identify these biases and fix them. The authors created three organizational frameworks covering how to measure bias, what test datasets exist to catch it, and what techniques can reduce it at different stages of model development. Understanding these problems matters because these systems increasingly influence important decisions affecting real people's lives.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models face risks from embedded social biases that can harm users and create legal exposure. This survey provides a structured framework for understanding bias problems and solutions across the entire model lifecycle. Decision makers should use these taxonomies to evaluate which mitigation strategies fit their development stage and risk tolerance. The consolidated datasets enable systematic testing before deployment. Understanding these categorized approaches helps organizations implement fairness as a technical requirement alongside performance metrics, reducing reputational damage and ensuring systems treat all users equitably.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive survey consolidates bias evaluation and mitigation approaches for large language models through three taxonomies. The evaluation metrics taxonomy organizes assessment methods by operational level: embeddings, probability distributions, and text generation. The dataset taxonomy categorizes bias testing resources by structure and targeted harms while providing consolidated access to public benchmarks. The mitigation taxonomy classifies intervention techniques across four stages: preprocessing, in-training, intra-processing, and post-processing, with detailed subcategories. The work synthesizes recent research to clarify methodological relationships and identify research directions for reducing harmful bias propagation in language models.

papers.note: Coconut reasons in hidden state rather than words, which removes the readable trace auditors currently rely on.
papers.title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
papers.explain_beginner: When a chatbot solves a math or logic problem step by step, it usually writes out its reasoning in plain sentences before giving an answer, a habit called chain of thought. This paper asks whether a model could reason in a different way entirely, using its own internal numerical representations instead of words, and whether that could work better for problems that require exploring several possible paths before finding the right one. The authors built a system called Coconut that feeds a model's internal state back into itself as the next reasoning step, rather than translating that state into a sentence first. On logic puzzles that need real planning and backtracking, this approach reached higher accuracy than writing out reasoning in words, and it did so using far fewer computational steps. On grade school math problems the internal approach did not beat writing things out in words, so the benefit was not universal. The tradeoff is that this internal reasoning is invisible to a human reader, since there is no readable sentence to check.
papers.explain_business: This is early stage research, not a deployable feature, and no current commercial model uses this technique. But it points to a real tension worth tracking. A common way businesses gain confidence in an AI system's answer is by reading the step by step reasoning it produces along the way, and using that trail for auditing, debugging, or compliance review. This paper shows that reasoning does not have to be produced as readable text to work, and in some cases works better and faster when it is not. If latent reasoning like this eventually reaches production systems, it would improve speed and possibly accuracy on planning heavy tasks, but it would also remove the readable trace that today lets a human or an automated checker verify how an answer was reached. Anyone building governance or audit processes around chain of thought output should treat that visibility as a current convenience rather than a permanent guarantee, since the field is actively exploring reasoning methods that do not produce it at all.
papers.explain_practitioner: Coconut replaces explicit chain of thought tokens with the model's last hidden state, fed back in as the next input embedding, so reasoning happens in continuous latent space rather than in language. Training uses a multi stage curriculum that starts from ordinary text based chain of thought and gradually swaps early reasoning steps for blocks of continuous thoughts, with the optimizer reset at each stage. The authors evaluate on GSM8k for arithmetic word problems, ProntoQA for simple multi hop logical inference, and a new benchmark they built called ProsQA, which uses graphs of logical relationships with distractor branches to force genuine search rather than pattern matching. On the harder planning heavy tasks, ProntoQA and ProsQA, Coconut matched or beat standard chain of thought while producing far shorter outputs. On GSM8k it underperformed chain of thought on raw accuracy. The authors are explicit that the curriculum is not optional. A version trained without it performed no better than skipping reasoning entirely, and scaling to a larger Llama 3 model produced smaller gains than on the smaller GPT-2 base.

papers.note: Changing only the numbers in a maths question degraded every model tested, and adding one irrelevant clause cut performance by up to 65 percent. Widely cited as evidence that benchmark scores overstate reasoning.
papers.title: GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether popular AI systems can actually do math reasoning or if they're just pattern-matching what they've seen before. They created new math problems by changing numbers and adding extra information to existing questions. They found that all tested AI models performed worse when numbers changed, even though the math stayed the same. Adding one unnecessary sentence dropped accuracy by up to 65 percent. This suggests the models aren't truly reasoning mathematically but instead copying shortcuts learned during training.
papers.explain_business: Organizations relying on LLMs for quantitative work should recognize that benchmark scores substantially overstate actual reasoning reliability. Models demonstrate fragility when encountering slightly unfamiliar problem variations or irrelevant information, which reflects real-world conditions. This has implications for deploying these systems in financial analysis, data interpretation, or problem-solving tasks where genuine mathematical reasoning is critical. Decision-makers should implement additional validation and human oversight rather than trusting published performance metrics as indicators of robust reasoning ability.
papers.explain_practitioner: We developed GSM-Symbolic, a benchmark generating diverse problem instantiations from symbolic templates to evaluate mathematical reasoning more rigorously than existing datasets like GSM8K. Testing state-of-the-art open and closed models revealed significant performance variance across different numerical values in identical problem structures. Models exhibited substantial degradation when problem complexity increased or irrelevant clauses were introduced, suggesting they lack genuine logical reasoning and instead rely on memorized patterns. These findings indicate current benchmarks significantly overestimate actual reasoning capabilities.

papers.note: Separates formal linguistic competence, knowing the rules, from functional competence, using language in the world, and argues models are strong on the first and patchy on the second. The distinction is now standard vocabulary in the debate.
papers.title: Dissociating language and thought in large language models
papers.explain_beginner: When a chatbot writes a fluent, grammatically perfect paragraph, does that mean it is actually thinking, reasoning, and understanding the world the way a person does? This paper asks that question by borrowing an idea from brain science. Researchers have found that in the human brain, the parts that handle grammar and word choice are largely separate from the parts that handle logic, math, memory for facts, and understanding other people's intentions. People who lose almost all language ability after a stroke can still play chess or solve arithmetic problems, showing language and thought are not the same thing. The authors argue today's large language models show the same split. They are remarkably good at producing grammatical sentences, matching human performance on tests of tricky grammar rules. But they are much weaker and inconsistent at logical reasoning, keeping facts straight, tracking who did what in a story, and reading between the lines in conversation. Fluent language, the paper concludes, is not proof of real understanding.
papers.explain_business: For anyone evaluating AI systems for business use, the practical takeaway is to stop treating fluent, well written output as evidence of correct reasoning or reliable factual recall. A model that writes flawless prose can still miscalculate a budget, contradict itself across a long document, or misread the intent behind a customer's message, because the skill that makes it read as competent is not the same skill that makes it correct. This argues for pairing language models with separate tools built for the actual task, a calculator or code execution for math, a retrieval system for facts, and structured checks for anything where being wrong carries a cost. It also means benchmark scores on language fluency or grammar tell buyers very little about reasoning reliability, so procurement and evaluation should test the specific functional skill a use case needs, such as multi-step logic or consistent entity tracking, rather than relying on general language quality as a proxy for trustworthiness.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors build their argument by mapping decades of cognitive neuroscience showing that the brain's language network, concentrated in left frontal and temporal regions, is functionally distinct from the networks supporting reasoning, world knowledge, and social cognition, then use that framework to review evidence on large language models. On formal linguistic competence, they cite strong results such as roughly 86 percent accuracy on the BLiMP grammaticality benchmark, close to human performance, plus evidence that model representations predict brain responses in the language network. On functional competence, the picture is uneven, models falter on arithmetic beyond a couple of digits, hallucinate facts, lose track of entities across a discourse, and fail theory of mind tests once simple control conditions are added. A key limitation the authors flag is that many headline claims about LLM reasoning or theory of mind come from fine-tuned or prompted models rather than base next word predictors, which conflates the two competences and can produce both overclaiming and underclaiming about what these systems can do.

papers.note: Reaches 100 percent jailbreak success across the major frontier models using simple adaptive search.
papers.title: Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers discovered that even the most advanced AI chatbots with built-in safety features can be tricked into ignoring their guidelines using relatively straightforward techniques. By adding carefully crafted text snippets to requests, attackers achieved a perfect success rate against every major commercial AI model tested. This matters because it reveals that current safety protections are weaker than assumed, highlighting the need for better defenses before these systems become more widely deployed.
papers.explain_business: Leading AI providers have safety systems that can be completely bypassed using simple, reproducible methods. Organizations deploying these models should recognize that published safety benchmarks may not reflect real-world robustness. This informs procurement decisions and risk assessments: current guardrails require substantial improvement before handling sensitive applications. The reproducible nature of these attacks means competitors or malicious actors can easily replicate bypasses, making immediate investment in robust defense mechanisms a strategic priority.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study demonstrates adaptive jailbreaking via random search optimization on model logprobs. For models exposing logprobs, researchers designed adversarial templates and appended optimized suffixes targeting high probability of unsafe tokens like 'Sure'. For models without logprob access, transfer attacks and prefilling exploits achieved equivalent success. Critical finding: adaptation to each model's architecture and API characteristics proved essential. They achieved 100% success across GPT-4o, Llama-3, Gemma, Claude variants, and 10+ other frontier models, including R2D2 specifically adversarially trained against prior GCG attacks.

papers.note: Formal proof parsing shows models handle single deduction steps but fail at proof planning, a precise statement of the limit.
papers.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether large language models actually reason logically or just appear to by following shortcuts. They created a fake world with logical rules and asked AI models to solve problems step-by-step. The models could handle individual logical steps correctly, but struggled when they needed to plan ahead and choose which steps to try first. This shows the models have some reasoning ability but lack genuine problem-solving strategy.
papers.explain_business: While large language models demonstrate genuine reasoning ability for individual logical steps, they cannot effectively plan complex multi-step solutions when alternatives exist. Organizations relying on these models for intricate problem-solving should recognize this limitation. The finding suggests current models work best for tasks with constrained reasoning paths, not open-ended planning, informing deployment strategy and expectations for autonomous reasoning applications.
papers.explain_practitioner: We developed PrOntoQA, a synthetic dataset grounded in first-order logic, to formally analyze chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs. By parsing generated proofs into symbolic form, we evaluated InstructGPT and GPT-3 on logical deduction tasks. Results reveal models successfully execute single inference steps but fail at proof planning, specifically when faced with multiple valid reasoning paths. This indicates limited search capability rather than fundamental reasoning deficiency.

papers.note: Early work defining representational bias sources and pushing the performance fairness frontier rather than trading one off.
papers.title: Towards Understanding and Mitigating Social Biases in Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models, which power many AI systems used in healthcare and law, can unintentionally learn and spread harmful stereotypes about gender, race, and religion from their training data. This paper identifies where these biases come from, creates tests to measure them, and develops techniques to reduce bias while keeping the AI systems working well. The researchers show their approach successfully removes unfair stereotypes without making the systems less capable.
papers.explain_business: This work addresses a critical risk for organizations deploying language models in consequential domains like healthcare and legal services, where biased outputs could cause real harm. The paper provides practical measurement tools and mitigation techniques that reduce stereotype propagation without sacrificing model quality. This enables responsible deployment while maintaining competitive performance, reducing regulatory and reputational risk.
papers.explain_practitioner: We systematized sources of representational bias in pretrained language models and developed new benchmarks and metrics for quantification. We then proposed mitigation strategies for bias during text generation. Our approach, validated through both automatic metrics and human evaluation, achieves bias reduction while maintaining high-quality output and contextual fidelity, advancing the Pareto frontier between fairness and performance objectives.

papers.note: Finds larger models produce less faithful reasoning traces, an inverse scaling result with direct governance consequences.
papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.explain_beginner: When AI systems explain their thinking step-by-step before answering questions, they often perform better. However, this research discovered that these explanations may not actually reflect how the model reached its answer. Scientists tested this by changing the explanations and seeing if the model's final answer changed. Surprisingly, bigger, more powerful models were often less truthful about their reasoning than smaller ones, which has important implications for trusting AI systems.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models for high-stakes decisions should be cautious about trusting the reasoning explanations these systems provide, particularly with larger models. The research indicates that bigger models may mask their actual decision-making processes while appearing to provide detailed explanations. Companies need to carefully select appropriate model sizes and tasks for their applications, actively validate that explanations reflect true reasoning, and avoid over-reliance on step-by-step explanations as proof of model trustworthiness without additional verification.
papers.explain_practitioner: We evaluated CoT faithfulness by measuring how much model predictions shift when the reasoning trace is modified through interventions like error injection or rephrasing. Testing across multiple tasks revealed heterogeneous conditioning behavior, where some tasks showed strong dependence on CoT while others showed minimal reliance. We identified that performance gains do not derive from increased computation or specific linguistic formulation. The study demonstrates an inverse scaling relationship, where larger models exhibit lower faithfulness on most evaluated tasks, indicating that task selection and model scale are critical factors for obtaining reliable reasoning explanations.

papers.note: Restricts to studies reporting actual safety outcomes rather than model accuracy, and finds no standardised benchmark exists.
papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Patient Safety Outcomes: Systematic Literature Review
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers examined studies about how artificial intelligence helps keep patients safe in hospitals and clinics. They found fifty-three studies showing that AI systems can catch medical errors, identify high-risk patients, and prevent medication problems. However, the studies used different methods to measure success, making it hard to compare results. The review shows AI has real promise for patient safety, but hospitals need better ways to test these systems before widely adopting them.
papers.explain_business: AI applications can meaningfully improve patient safety through better error detection and medication management, representing valuable risk mitigation opportunities. However, organizations should recognize that existing published systems lack standardized evaluation metrics, making it difficult to assess which solutions deliver genuine clinical value. Before implementing AI systems, executives should prioritize vendors demonstrating real-world validation data and ensuring solutions have been tested in actual clinical environments rather than relying solely on algorithm accuracy metrics.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review analyzed fifty-three quantitative studies integrating machine learning and natural language processing for patient safety outcomes between 2009 and 2019. Studies focused on three areas: clinical alarms using decision trees, clinical reports using support vector machines, and drug safety using decision trees. Key findings revealed that while AI-enabled decision support systems improved error detection and patient stratification, significant heterogeneity existed in both AI methodology and performance reporting. Critically, no standardized evaluation benchmark was identified, limiting cross-study comparison and clinical validation.

papers.note: First sparse model to reach state of the art on transfer learning, and a practical design guide for instability.
papers.title: ST-MoE: Designing Stable and Transferable Sparse Expert Models
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers developed a new approach to building very large language models that use less energy than traditional methods. The key challenge was that these efficient models were unstable and didn't work well when adapted to new tasks. This paper provides solutions to these problems and demonstrates that their improved model outperforms competitors on many important language tasks, from question-answering to summarization, while using significantly less computational power.
papers.explain_business: This work enables deploying language models with vastly more capacity while reducing infrastructure costs. A 269-billion parameter model runs with the computational footprint of a much smaller system, directly improving cost-efficiency in production deployments. The demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across multiple real-world tasks means organizations can achieve better results on reasoning, summarization, and question-answering applications without proportionally increasing operational expenses.
papers.explain_practitioner: We addressed training instability and transfer learning degradation in Mixture-of-Experts sparse models through systematic design improvements. We scaled ST-MoE to 269B parameters while maintaining computational efficiency equivalent to a 32B dense Transformer. The model achieved state-of-the-art results across diverse benchmarks including SuperGLUE, ARC, XSum, CNN-DM, WebQA, Natural Questions, Winogrande, and ANLI R3, representing the first sparse model to reach this performance level in transfer learning scenarios.

papers.note: Added because a reader's question on this site drew on it (1 time so far). The page exists so the next reader finds it in the answer.
papers.title: Energy and Policy Considerations for Deep Learning in NLP
papers.authors: Emma Strubell, Ananya Ganesh, Andrew McCallum
papers.abstract: Recent progress in hardware and methodology for training neural networks has ushered in a new generation of large networks trained on abundant data. These models have obtained notable gains in accuracy across many NLP tasks. However, these accuracy improvements depend on the availability of exceptionally large computational resources that necessitate similarly substantial energy consumption. As a result these models are costly to train and develop, both financially, due to the cost of hardware and electricity or cloud compute time, and environmentally, due to the carbon footprint required to fuel modern tensor processing hardware. In this paper we bring this issue to the attention of NLP researchers by quantifying the approximate financial and environmental costs of training a variety of recently successful neural network models for NLP. Based on these findings, we propose actionable recommendations to reduce costs and improve equity in NLP research and practice.
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines the hidden costs of modern language AI systems. While these systems have become remarkably good at understanding text, training them requires enormous amounts of electricity and expensive computer hardware. The researchers measured how much energy and money it takes to build popular AI language models, revealing that these expenses create barriers for researchers without access to well-funded labs. They then suggest practical ways to make this technology more accessible and environmentally responsible.
papers.explain_business: Training advanced language AI models demands substantial capital investment in specialized hardware and energy costs, creating competitive advantages for well-resourced organizations. This paper quantifies those expenses and demonstrates how resource constraints limit who can participate in AI development. For businesses, the findings suggest that operational efficiency and cost reduction in model training directly impact competitiveness. The recommendations indicate that optimizing training approaches not only reduces expenses but also expands the potential talent pool by lowering barriers to entry for smaller competitors and academic institutions.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors quantified the computational, financial, and carbon costs associated with training state-of-the-art neural language models. They measured electricity consumption and hardware expenses across several prominent NLP architectures trained on large datasets. Their analysis demonstrated significant disparities in resource requirements and accessibility. The paper provides specific cost metrics for different model types and training approaches, then offers evidence-based recommendations for practitioners to reduce resource consumption and improve equity in model development and research.

papers.note: Shows frontier reasoning models collapse completely past a complexity threshold, the strongest evidence yet against vendor reasoning claims.
papers.title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
papers.explain_beginner: New AI models claim to show their thinking before answering questions. This study tested whether they actually think better than older models. Using puzzle games with different difficulty levels, researchers found these reasoning models perform well on medium-difficulty tasks but completely fail on harder problems. Surprisingly, they stop trying harder even when they could, suggesting their claimed thinking process has real limits that companies haven't fully disclosed.
papers.explain_business: Organizations considering investments in advanced reasoning models should recognize they perform reliably only on medium-difficulty problems. Beyond that threshold, performance degrades completely, regardless of additional computational resources. This directly impacts use cases requiring complex analysis or high-stakes decision support. Decision-makers should evaluate actual performance ceilings for their specific problem domains rather than relying on vendor benchmarks, as claimed reasoning improvements may not translate to real-world applications.
papers.explain_practitioner: We evaluated Large Reasoning Models using controlled puzzle environments enabling precise complexity manipulation. Analysis included final accuracy and reasoning traces across three regimes: low-complexity favors standard LLMs, medium-complexity favors LRMs, and high-complexity causes total collapse in both. LRMs exhibit token budget decline despite available capacity and struggle with exact computation and algorithmic reasoning. This reveals fundamental limitations in current reasoning architectures beyond benchmark contamination issues.

papers.note: Compares open source and proprietary medical models and the metrics used to judge them.
papers.title: Large language models in healthcare and medical domain: A review
papers.explain_beginner: This paper surveys how advanced AI language models are being used in healthcare. These models can read and understand medical questions and information remarkably well. The researchers reviewed what these models can do, from identifying medical terms in documents to answering patient questions, and compared different models available to hospitals and clinics. They also explained the measurements used to determine whether these models work properly and identified obstacles that still need solving before widespread use.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations considering LLM deployment should understand that these systems can meaningfully improve clinical documentation processing and information retrieval. This review enables decision-makers to evaluate available options by comparing proprietary versus open-source models and understanding how to measure their performance. However, organizations should recognize significant limitations and constraints remain. The findings indicate LLMs offer genuine efficiency potential in healthcare operations but require careful assessment of specific use cases and ongoing research before large-scale implementation.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive review examines LLM applications across healthcare tasks including named entity recognition, relation extraction, natural language inference, multimodal analysis, document classification, and question-answering. The authors trace development from traditional pretrained language models through current LLMs, evaluate state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source models, and detail performance metrics for biomedical evaluation. The work synthesizes existing healthcare LLM functionalities, assesses comparative effectiveness across implementations, and identifies technical limitations and implementation challenges requiring further research and development.

papers.note: Reviews student and teacher assistance, adaptive learning and commercial tools, with the datasets and benchmarks behind each, plus the deployment risks.
papers.title: Large Language Models for Education: A survey and outlook
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines how large language models, the technology behind tools like ChatGPT, can improve education. Researchers looked at how these AI systems help both students and teachers, personalize learning for individual needs, and reviewed existing educational products using this technology. They also identified potential problems with using these tools in schools and suggested areas for future improvement. The work matters because it helps educators understand how to responsibly adopt this powerful technology to create better learning experiences.
papers.explain_business: This analysis demonstrates that LLM-based educational tools span multiple market segments from student assistance to teacher augmentation to adaptive learning platforms. Understanding the datasets and benchmarks used to evaluate these systems helps stakeholders assess technology maturity and competitive positioning. The documented deployment risks and challenges indicate where regulatory compliance and safety mechanisms become necessary business considerations. For educational institutions and edtech companies, this roadmap clarifies which applications are production-ready versus requiring further development before implementation.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey systematically reviews LLM applications across educational domains including student tutoring, teacher support, and personalized instruction systems. The authors catalog relevant datasets, benchmarks, and technological implementations across each application area. The study identifies and categorizes deployment challenges and safety concerns specific to educational contexts. Key findings include assessment of current commercial solutions and their underlying capabilities, gaps in existing evaluation frameworks, and research priorities for advancing educational AI systems responsibly.

papers.note: Peer reviewed survey linking architecture choices to downstream limitations across biomedicine, vision language and code.
papers.title: Large language models (LLMs): survey, technical frameworks, and future challenges
papers.explain_beginner: This paper surveys large language models, which are advanced AI systems that understand and generate human language. The research reviews how these models work, examines their use across different fields like medicine, image understanding, and software coding, and explores what they do well and where they fall short. The findings help readers understand current AI capabilities and suggest areas needing improvement for future progress.
papers.explain_business: This survey identifies where large language models currently succeed and fail across practical applications including medical analysis, visual understanding, and software development.
